questions.stemHtml: In given radiological anatomy image identify the thalamus?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) C

 

  1. The thalamus is a large, egg-shaped structure located in the central region of the brain.
  2. It serves as a major relay station for sensory and motor signals to the cerebral cortex.
  3. In the sagittal section provided, C corresponds to the thalamus.

 

Identification of the Other Labels:

 

  • A: Corpus callosum (superior to the thalamus, connecting the two cerebral hemispheres).
  • B: Fornix (a white matter tract involved in the limbic system, beneath the corpus callosum).
  • D: Hypothalamus (inferior and anterior to the thalamus, involved in homeostasis and autonomic control).
  • E: Pituitary gland (connected to the hypothalamus via the infundibulum, responsible for hormone regulation).

 

Educational Objective:

 

In radiological anatomy, the thalamus is identified as the large, centrally located structure, marked as C in this image.

questions.stemHtml: Lesion to indicated structure will result in paralysis of which of the following muscle
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Risoreus 

 

The indicated structure in the image is the facial colliculus, located in the floor of the fourth ventricle. This elevation is caused by the abducens nerve nucleus (cranial nerve VI) and the fibers of the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) that loop around it.

 

Effects of Lesion to the Facial Colliculus:

 

  • Facial Nerve (VII):
    • The axons of the facial nerve pass superficially over the colliculus.
    • A lesion will primarily affect the muscles of facial expression, including Risorius, which is involved in smiling.
  • Abducens Nerve (VI):
    • The nucleus of the abducens nerve, located at the colliculus, controls the lateral rectus muscle (responsible for lateral movement of the eye).
    • Damage to this nucleus can lead to paralysis of the lateral rectus muscle, causing medial deviation of the eye (esotropia).
  • Controlled by the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII). Damage to the facial colliculus will lead to paralysis of facial muscles, including Risorius, which is responsible for producing a "smiling" expression. Correct.

 

Option Analysis

 

Option A. Medial rectus: Controlled by the oculomotor nerve (cranial nerve III), which is not related to the facial colliculus. Incorrect.

 

Option B. Lateral rectus: While the abducens nucleus is part of the facial colliculus, the facial nerve fibers looping over the colliculus are more superficial. Damage typically impacts facial nerve functions first. A secondary effect may involve the lateral rectus, but Risorius is the better answer.

 

Option C. Superior rectus: Controlled by the oculomotor nerve, which is unrelated to the facial colliculus. Incorrect.

 

Educational Objective:

 

A lesion to the facial colliculus will primarily affect the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII), causing paralysis of muscles of facial expression such as Risorius. The lateral rectus muscle (abducens nerve, cranial nerve VI) may also be affected secondarily, but facial muscles take precedence.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old girl is admitted to the hospital with severe dyspnea. Physical examination reveals that the patient is suffering from an asthma attack, with associated bronchospasm. Which of the following nerves is responsible for the innervation of the bronchial smooth muscle cells?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Vagus

 

The vagus nerve (cranial nerve X) is part of the parasympathetic nervous system and plays a central role in the innervation of the bronchial smooth muscle cells. The vagus nerve releases acetylcholine, which acts on muscarinic receptors in the bronchial smooth muscle. This can lead to bronchoconstriction, as seen in asthma attacks, where hyperresponsiveness of the airway smooth muscle occurs.

 

During an asthma attack, stimulation of the vagus nerve exacerbates bronchospasm by increasing contraction of the bronchial smooth muscle. This is a hallmark mechanism of asthma that contributes to airway narrowing and difficulty breathing.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Greater thoracic splanchnic: The greater thoracic splanchnic nerve is part of the sympathetic nervous system and provides innervation to abdominal organs, including parts of the digestive tract. It does not directly innervate bronchial smooth muscle.

 

Option B. Phrenic: The phrenic nerve primarily innervates the diaphragm, playing a critical role in respiration by enabling diaphragmatic contraction. It does not control bronchial smooth muscle.

 

Option D. Lesser thoracic splanchnic: Similar to the greater thoracic splanchnic nerve, the lesser thoracic splanchnic nerve is involved in sympathetic innervation of abdominal structures. It does not innervate bronchial smooth muscle.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The vagus nerve is responsible for the parasympathetic innervation of bronchial smooth muscle cells, causing bronchoconstriction through activation of muscarinic receptors. This mechanism is central to asthma-related bronchospasm.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is the action of indicated muscle:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Protraction

 

  • The indicated muscle in the image is the lateral pterygoid muscle, which is located in the region of the lateral pterygoid plate in the transverse section of the face.
  • This muscle is involved in movements of the temporomandibular joint (TMJ).
  • Protraction is the primary action of the lateral pterygoid, making it the best answer.

 

Actions of the Lateral Pterygoid Muscle:  mnemonic dsp

 

Protraction:

 

  • The lateral pterygoid pulls the mandible forward during jaw opening. This is its primary action.
  • It achieves this by pulling the mandibular condyle forward, allowing the mouth to open fully.

 

Depression:

 

  • Assists in jaw opening by depressing the mandible in combination with other muscles like the digastric muscle.
  • However, the digastric and geniohyoid muscles are considered stronger depressors, so protraction takes priority.

 

Side-to-Side Movement (Lateral Excursion):

 

  • When the lateral pterygoid acts unilaterally, it moves the mandible side-to-side.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Retraction: Opposite of protraction, controlled by the posterior fibers of the temporalis muscle, not the lateral pterygoid. Incorrect.

 

Option C. Elevation: Elevation is controlled by muscles like the temporalis, masseter, and medial pterygoid, not the lateral pterygoid. Incorrect.

 

Option D. Depression: Though the lateral pterygoid assists in depression, it is secondary to protraction. The strongest depressors are the geniohyoid and digastric muscles, making this option less accurate.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The lateral pterygoid muscle is primarily responsible for protraction of the mandible during jaw movements.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old male who fell from a tree complains of severe pain over the right side of his chest because of a rib fracture at the midaxillary line. He is admitted to the hospital due to his difficulty breathing. Radiographic and physical examinations reveal atelectasis, resulting from the accumulation of blood in his pleural space and resulting hemothorax. What is the most likely the source of bleeding to cause the hemothorax?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Intercostal vessels

 

The intercostal vessels run along the inferior border of each rib, within the costal groove, and are responsible for supplying blood to the intercostal muscles and adjacent tissues. A rib fracture at the midaxillary line is highly likely to damage these vessels, resulting in bleeding into the pleural space (hemothorax).

 

The accumulation of blood in the pleural space increases intrathoracic pressure, leading to lung collapse (atelectasis) and difficulty breathing. The intercostal vessels are particularly vulnerable in this scenario due to their proximity to the ribs, especially in fractures.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Left common carotid artery: This artery supplies blood to the head and neck. It is located far from the ribs and is not relevant to a rib fracture or hemothorax.

 

Option C. Pulmonary arteries: These arteries carry deoxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs and are located deep within the thorax. While they can cause significant bleeding if damaged, they are not typically affected by rib fractures at the midaxillary line.

 

Option D. Internal thoracic artery: This artery runs along the posterior aspect of the anterior chest wall, near the sternum. It is not located near the midaxillary line and is less likely to be injured in this scenario.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In cases of rib fractures, the intercostal vessels are the most common source of bleeding leading to a hemothorax, due to their location along the inferior border of the ribs in the costal groove.

questions.stem: In Pringle’s menuvere method which anatomical structure is mainly compressed
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Portal vein & hepatic artery

 

1. Purpose of Pringle’s Maneuver:

 

  • It is a surgical technique used to temporarily control bleeding from the liver during trauma or surgery.
  • The maneuver involves compressing the hepatoduodenal ligament, which contains key vascular structures.

 

 

2. Anatomy of the Hepatoduodenal Ligament:

 

  • The hepatoduodenal ligament is the free edge of the lesser omentum.
  • It contains three structures collectively referred to as VAD:
    • V: Portal vein.
    • A: Hepatic artery.
    • D: Common bile duct.

 

3. Structures Compressed:

 

  • By applying pressure on the hepatoduodenal ligament, the following structures are compressed:
    • Portal vein: Major venous drainage of the gastrointestinal tract to the liver.
    • Hepatic artery: Arterial supply to the liver.

 

4. Structures Not Compressed:

 

  • Hepatic vein: Drains blood from the liver into the inferior vena cava and is not located in the hepatoduodenal ligament, so it is not affected by Pringle’s maneuver.

 

Educational Objective:

 

During Pringle’s maneuver, the portal vein and hepatic artery are compressed by clamping the hepatoduodenal ligament, effectively controlling liver bleeding. D is the correct answer.

questions.stem: Fusion of the caudal portions of the kidneys during embryonic development is most likely to result in which of the following congenital conditions?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Horseshoe kidney

 

A horseshoe kidney occurs due to the fusion of the caudal (lower) poles of the kidneys during embryonic development. As a result, the kidneys become connected, usually at the level of the L3-L4 vertebrae. This anomaly prevents normal ascent of the kidneys during development because the fused structure gets trapped under the inferior mesenteric artery. Despite its abnormal position, the horseshoe kidney typically functions normally, though it may increase the risk of complications like infections or stones.

 

Fusion of the caudal poles is a hallmark feature of this condition, making horseshoe kidney the most appropriate answer.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Bicornuate uterus: This condition results from incomplete fusion of the paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts during female embryogenesis and is unrelated to kidney development.

 

Option B. Cryptorchidism: Cryptorchidism is the failure of one or both testes to descend into the scrotum. It is related to the development of the testes and their associated structures, not the kidneys.

 

Option D. Renal agenesis: Renal agenesis occurs when one or both kidneys fail to develop. It is a separate congenital defect caused by disruptions in the metanephric blastema or ureteric bud formation, not due to caudal fusion.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Fusion of the caudal poles of the kidneys during development results in a horseshoe kidney, which is typically located at or below the L3-L4 level due to entrapment by the inferior mesenteric artery.

questions.stem: Portal vein is formed at level of?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) L2 

 

Formation of the Portal Vein:

 

1. Components:

 

  • The portal vein is formed by the union of the superior mesenteric vein (SMV) and the splenic vein.
  • Sometimes, the inferior mesenteric vein (IMV) also drains into the splenic vein before contributing to the portal vein.

 

 

2. Level of Formation:

 

  • This union occurs behind the neck of the pancreas at the vertebral level L2.

 

 

3. Clinical Significance:

 

  • The portal vein is a crucial part of the portal circulation, carrying blood from the gastrointestinal tract, spleen, pancreas, and gallbladder to the liver.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The portal vein is formed at the L2 vertebral level, behind the neck of the pancreas, by the union of the superior mesenteric vein (SMV) and the splenic vein.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old male is admitted to the emergency department with severe upper abdominal pain. Gastroscopy reveals a tumor in the antrum of the stomach. A CT scan is ordered to evaluate lymphatic drainage of the stomach. Which of the following lymph nodes is most likely to be involved in a malignancy of the stomach?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Celiac

 

The celiac lymph nodes are the primary lymphatic drainage site for the stomach, particularly for the regions including the antrum. The stomach drains lymph into several nodes, but the celiac nodes are the central collecting point, especially for malignancies. From the celiac nodes, cancer cells may further spread to other lymphatic areas or distant organs.

 

The celiac lymph nodes are anatomically situated near the celiac trunk, the main arterial supply of the stomach, which aligns with their role as the primary lymphatic hub.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Superior mesenteric: These nodes drain lymph from the midgut structures, such as the small intestine, cecum, and parts of the colon. They are not involved in stomach lymphatic drainage.

 

Option C. Inferior mesenteric: These nodes drain the hindgut structures, including the descending colon, sigmoid colon, and rectum. They are unrelated to stomach lymphatic drainage.

 

Option D. Hepatic: The hepatic lymph nodes primarily receive drainage from the liver, gallbladder, and parts of the bile ducts. They are not the primary site for lymphatic drainage of the stomach.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The celiac lymph nodes are the primary lymphatic drainage nodes for the stomach and are most likely to be involved in malignancies originating from the stomach.

questions.stemHtml: The appearance of the colon on double contrast barium enema examination is shown in image. Identify the A,B & C respectively

options.label: A
options.text: Hepatic flexure, splenic flexure, transverse colon

options.label: C
options.text: Splenic flexure, Hepatic flexure, , transverse colon

questions.answerText: Splenic flexure, Hepatic flexure, , transverse colon
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Splenic  flexure, Hepatic flexure, , transverse colon

 

Identifications in the Image:

 

  1. Colon Characteristics:
    • The large intestine can be identified on imaging due to features like haustra (pouch-like structures), appendices epiploicae, and taeniae coli.
  2. Barium Enema Study:
    • The study highlights the anatomy of the large intestine and its distinctive segments.
    • Flexures (hepatic and splenic):
      • Hepatic flexure: Located on the right side near the liver.
      • Splenic flexure: Located on the left side near the spleen.
    • Transverse colon runs horizontally between these two flexures.

 

Analysing the Labels (A, B, C):

 

Option A. Located near the right side of the abdomen, adjacent to the liver. This indicates the hepatic flexure.

 

Option B. Positioned near the left side of the abdomen, adjacent to the spleen. This corresponds to the splenic flexure.

 

Option C. The horizontal portion connecting A (hepatic flexure) and B (splenic flexure). This is the transverse colon.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In a double-contrast barium enema, the anatomical sequence of the large intestine in the image aligns with hepatic flexure (A), splenic flexure (B), and transverse colon (C).

questions.stem: A 45-year-old male entered the emergency department with a complaint of severe abdominal pain. During physical examination it is observed that his cremasteric reflex is absent. Which of the following nerves is responsible for the efferent limb of the cremasteric reflex?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Genitofemoral

 

The cremasteric reflex involves the following components:

 

  1. Receptor: Skin of the femoral triangle, stimulated by touch.
  2. Afferent limb: Femoral branch of the genitofemoral nerve and the ilioinguinal nerve.
  3. Center: Reflex arc in the spinal cord segments L1-L2.
  4. Efferent limb: Genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve.
  5. Effector muscle: Cremaster muscle, which contracts to elevate the testis.

 

 

In this question, the absence of the reflex indicates disruption in the efferent pathway, which is mediated by the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve.

 

Other Options

 

Option A. Ilioinguinal: The ilioinguinal nerve is responsible for carrying sensory input from the skin of the femoral triangle and does not contribute to the motor (efferent) limb of the reflex.

 

Option B. Iliohypogastric: The iliohypogastric nerve provides sensation to the lower abdominal wall but is not involved in the cremasteric reflex.

 

Option D. Pudendal: The pudendal nerve is primarily responsible for innervation of the perineum and does not play a role in the cremasteric reflex.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The afferent limb of cremasteric reflex is by femoral branch of genitofemoral nerve and the efferent limb of the cremasteric reflex is mediated by the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve. Overall, the cremasteric reflex is governed by the genitofemoral nerve (L1-L2).

questions.stemHtml: At which level of brain, the nucleus supplying to the marked muscle is situated?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Superior colliculus

 

Marked Muscle in the Image:

 

  • The muscle indicated in the diagram is the medial rectus, one of the extraocular muscles responsible for adduction of the eyeball.
  • The medial rectus muscle is innervated by the oculomotor nerve (cranial nerve III).

 

Nucleus of Cranial Nerve III:

 

  • The oculomotor nerve nucleus is located in the midbrain at the level of the superior colliculus.
  • The nerve controls most of the extraocular muscles, including the medial rectus, superior rectus, inferior rectus, and inferior oblique, along with the levator palpebrae superioris.

 

Colliculi Levels:

 

  • Superior colliculus: Associated with the oculomotor nucleus (cranial nerve III).
  • Inferior colliculus: Associated with the trochlear nucleus (cranial nerve IV), which supplies the superior oblique muscle.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Facial colliculus: Located in the pons, related to cranial nerve VII (facial nerve) and cranial nerve VI (abducens nerve).

 

Option C. Inferior colliculus: Associated with cranial nerve IV.

 

Option D. Inferior olivary nucleus: Located in the medulla, not involved in eye movement or cranial nerve III.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The oculomotor nerve nucleus lies at the level of the superior colliculus in the midbrain. This is the key to answering questions related to the medial rectus muscle.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old patient is admitted to the hospital after suffering a ruptured spleen in a skiing accident. Physical examination reveals intense pain that radiates to the region of the left shoulder, presumably due to irritation of the diaphragm. Which of the following signs best describes this condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Kehr sign

 

Kehr sign refers to referred pain in the left shoulder caused by irritation of the diaphragm. This phenomenon occurs because the phrenic nerve, which innervates the diaphragm, shares the same spinal segments (C3, C4, C5) as the supraclavicular nerves that supply sensation to the shoulder region. In this case, the ruptured spleen leads to blood or irritation in the peritoneal cavity, which stimulates the diaphragm, resulting in referred pain to the left shoulder.

 

 

Other Options

 

Option A. Mittelschmerz: Mittelschmerz refers to unilateral pelvic pain associated with ovulation and has no relation to diaphragm irritation or referred shoulder pain.

 

Option C. Rovsing sign: Rovsing sign is associated with appendicitis and refers to pain in the right lower quadrant when pressure is applied to the left lower quadrant. It is unrelated to diaphragm or shoulder pain.

 

 

Option D. Psoas sign: Psoas sign is another clinical sign associated with appendicitis, caused by irritation of the psoas muscle, resulting in pain on hip flexion or extension. It does not involve the diaphragm or shoulder.

 

 

Educational Objective:

 

Kehr sign is the referred pain in the left shoulder due to irritation of the diaphragm, commonly caused by conditions such as ruptured spleen or diaphragmatic irritation, mediated via the phrenic nerve.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man is admitted to the hospital due to severe back pain. Radiographic examination reveals severe osteoporosis of the vertebral column, with crush fractures of vertebrae L4 and L5. Which of the following parts of the vertebrae are most likely to be fractured in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Vertebral bodies

 

In osteoporosis, the density and strength of bone are significantly reduced, making the vertebral bodies particularly susceptible to compression or crush fractures. The vertebral bodies bear the majority of the axial load in the spine, especially in the lumbar region (L4 and L5), which experiences high mechanical stress. Severe osteoporosis compromises the structural integrity of these load-bearing structures, leading to their collapse.

 

The intervertebral disks, although subject to wear and tear, do not "fracture" in the same way bones do. Disks may herniate or prolapse but are not implicated in fractures. Other bony parts like the spinous and transverse processes are less commonly involved unless there is significant trauma.

 

 

 

Other Options

 

Option A. Spinal process: The spinal processes are not typically affected in osteoporosis-related fractures unless there is significant trauma, as they are not primary load-bearing structures.

 

Option C. Transverse process: The transverse processes are also non-load-bearing structures and are less likely to be involved in crush fractures caused by osteoporosis.

 

Option D. Intervertebral disk: Intervertebral disks do not fracture but may undergo herniation or degeneration. This question specifically pertains to fractures of bony structures, not soft tissue injuries.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In osteoporosis, vertebral bodies are the most likely parts of the vertebrae to sustain crush fractures due to their role in bearing the axial load of the spine, especially in weight-bearing lumbar regions.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman is admitted to the emergency department after a car crash. Radiographic examination reveals a whiplash injury in addition to hyperextension of her cervical spine. Which of the following ligaments will most likely be injured?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Anterior longitudinal ligament

 

A whiplash injury commonly occurs during a car crash due to sudden acceleration and deceleration forces, leading to hyperextension of the cervical spine. During hyperextension, the anterior longitudinal ligament, which runs along the anterior aspect of the vertebral bodies, is subjected to excessive stretching and can become injured or torn. This ligament provides stability to the anterior vertebral column and prevents hyperextension under normal conditions.

 

 

In contrast, ligaments positioned posteriorly, such as the posterior longitudinal ligament and ligamentum flavum, are stretched during flexion rather than extension.

 

Other Options

 

Option A. Ligamentum flavum: This ligament runs along the posterior aspect of the vertebral canal and is responsible for maintaining the stability of the spine during flexion. It is not involved in injuries caused by hyperextension.

 

Option C. Posterior longitudinal ligament: This ligament lies within the vertebral canal along the posterior aspect of the vertebral bodies and is involved in stabilizing the spine during flexion. It is unlikely to be injured during hyperextension.

 

 

Option D. Anulus fibrosus: The anulus fibrosus is the outer fibrous ring of the intervertebral disks. While it may sustain damage in other conditions such as disk herniation, it is not directly involved in hyperextension injuries.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In hyperextension injuries of the cervical spine, such as those seen in whiplash injuries during car crashes, the anterior longitudinal ligament is most likely to be injured.

questions.stem: Most lateral nucleus of cerebellum?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Dentate

 

The cerebellum contains four deep nuclei arranged medially to laterally as follows:

 

  1. Fastigial (most medial)
  2. Globose
  3. Emboliform
  4. Dentate (most lateral and the largest).

 

 

The dentate nucleus is characterized by its tooth-like appearance (hence the name "dentate," derived from Latin for "tooth"). It is the most lateral of the cerebellar nuclei and plays a significant role in motor coordination and fine motor skills. 

 

Educational Objective:

 

The dentate nucleus is the most lateral and largest nucleus of the cerebellum and is essential for motor coordination.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man is admitted to the hospital after an injury sustained at work in a factory. He presents with severe scalp lacerations, which were sutured. After three days the wound is inflammed, swollen, and painful. Between which tissue layers is the infection most likely located?

options.label: C
options.text: The dense connective tissue and the aponeurosis

options.label: D
options.text: The dense connective tissue and the skin

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) The aponeurosis and the periosteum

 

The scalp consists of five distinct layers, often remembered by the acronym SCALP:

 

S - Skin

C - Connective tissue (dense)

A - Aponeurosis (galea aponeurotica)

L - Loose areolar connective tissue (the "danger zone")

P - Pericranium (periosteum)

 

 

The loose areolar connective tissue, located between the aponeurosis and the pericranium (periosteum), is known as the "danger zone" of the scalp. This layer provides a potential space where infections can spread easily, leading to inflammation, swelling, and pain. Bacteria or pathogens introduced through lacerations can travel quickly within this layer, making it the most common site for infection following a scalp injury.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. The periosteum and bone: Infection in this layer is rare unless the infection progresses from the loose areolar tissue to involve the pericranium and underlying bone. This is unlikely in the early stages of scalp wound infections.

 

Option C. The dense connective tissue and the aponeurosis: The dense connective tissue is tightly bound to the aponeurosis, making the spread of infection in this layer difficult.

 

Option D. The dense connective tissue and the skin: Infection in this layer would usually manifest as superficial cellulitis or an abscess but is not the typical layer for deeper scalp infections.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Infections following scalp lacerations typically localize in the loose areolar connective tissue, located between the aponeurosis and the pericranium, due to its potential space for fluid and pathogen spread.

questions.stemHtml: A kind of hernia is shown in the image. Which anatomical structure is not present in the boundary of related space?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Trapezius

 

The hernia shown in the image is a lumbar hernia, and the space being referred to is Petit’s triangle. This is a weak spot in the lumbar region where herniation can occur. 

 

 

The boundaries of Petit’s triangle are as follows:

 

  • Medial boundary: Latissimus dorsi (a large, broad muscle of the back).
  • Lateral boundary: External oblique muscle (part of the abdominal wall).
  • Inferior boundary: Iliac crest (the superior border of the hip bone).

 

The trapezius muscle, though located in the back, is not part of the boundaries of Petit’s triangle. Hence, it is not related to this hernia or its anatomical boundaries.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The trapezius muscle is not part of the boundaries of Petit’s triangle, which is a site for lumbar hernia formation. The boundaries are formed by the latissimus dorsi, external oblique, and iliac crest.

questions.stem: 54-year-old man was admitted to the emergency department after he was struck by an automobile. Radiographic examination revealed a fracture through the crista galli of the anterior cranial fossa, resulting in slow, local bleeding. Which of the following is the most likely source of bleeding?

options.label: B
options.text: The great cerebral vein of Galen

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Superior sagittal sinus

 

The crista galli is a bony projection of the ethmoid bone that provides an attachment point for the falx cerebri, a dural fold. The superior sagittal sinus runs along the upper margin of the falx cerebri and is located near the crista galli. A fracture through the crista galli can disrupt this sinus, causing venous bleeding. The superior sagittal sinus is a major dural venous sinus that collects blood from the cerebral veins and drains into the confluence of sinuses.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Middle meningeal artery: The middle meningeal artery supplies the dura mater and is typically associated with fractures in the temporal region involving the foramen spinosum or pterion, leading to epidural hematomas. It is not relevant to fractures near the crista galli.

 

Option B. The great cerebral vein of Galen: The great cerebral vein of Galen is located deeper in the brain near the confluence of the straight sinus and is not anatomically close to the crista galli or the anterior cranial fossa.

 

Option D. Superior ophthalmic vein: The superior ophthalmic vein is related to venous drainage from the orbit and is not typically involved in fractures near the crista galli or anterior cranial fossa.

 

Educational Objective:

 

A fracture through the crista galli of the anterior cranial fossa is most likely to cause bleeding from the superior sagittal sinus, a major venous sinus located near the falx cerebri attachment.

questions.stem: Chassaignac’s tubercle is related with which vertebra?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) C6

 

Chassaignac's tubercle refers to the anterior tubercle of the transverse process of the C6 vertebra. This structure is clinically significant as it is closely related to the common carotid artery, which is palpable at this level. The anterior tubercle serves as an important anatomical landmark for identifying the carotid artery during various medical procedures.

 

 

Additional points of interest:

 

  • The cricoid cartilage and cricopharyngeal junction are also located at the C6 vertebral level, further emphasizing its anatomical importance.
  • The tubercle is sometimes referred to as the carotid tubercle, highlighting its relationship with the common carotid artery.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Chassaignac's tubercle, also called the carotid tubercle, is the anterior tubercle of the transverse process of the C6 vertebra, and it is closely related to the common carotid artery, which is palpable at this level.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the anomaly:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Anencephaly

 

The image depicts a fetus with anencephaly, a congenital anomaly resulting from the failure of the anterior neuropore to close during embryonic development. This defect leads to the absence of a major portion of the brain, skull, and scalp. Key features in the image include the absence of cranial vault bones and the exposed brain tissue, which degenerates due to amniotic fluid exposure.

 

  • Cause: Anencephaly is a neural tube defect caused by incomplete closure of the cranial (anterior) neuropore.
  • Clinical Presentation: The fetus typically lacks a functional brain, and the cranial vault is absent. This condition is incompatible with life.

 

Other Options

 

Option B. Rachischisis: Rachischisis involves a failure of the posterior neuropore to close, resulting in an open spine. The defect is primarily seen along the back and does not involve the absence of the brain or cranial vault.

 

 

Option C. Craniorachischisis: Craniorachischisis is a severe form of neural tube defect where both the cranial (anterior) and spinal (posterior) neuropores fail to close, resulting in a combined absence of the brain and an open spinal defect. questions.stem: Thinnest cranial nerve is?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) IV cranial nerve

 

The fourth cranial nerve (trochlear nerve) is the thinnest cranial nerve, as it contains the least number of axons. This is because it only innervates one muscle, the superior oblique muscle (SO4, indicating the superior oblique is supplied by the fourth cranial nerve).

 

Unique features of the trochlear nerve include:

 

  • It is the only cranial nerve that decussates (crosses over) completely before exiting the brainstem.
  • It has a dorsal attachment (emerging from the dorsal surface of the midbrain), making it unique among cranial nerves.
  • It has the longest intracranial course, yet it is the thinnest due to the minimal number of axons required to innervate just one muscle.

 

These structural and functional aspects contribute to its classification as the thinnest cranial nerve.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. I cranial nerve (Olfactory nerve): Though it appears small, the olfactory nerve is not classified as the thinnest, and it is not associated with innervating a single muscle like the trochlear nerve.

 

Option C. VI cranial nerve (Abducens nerve): The abducens nerve is responsible for innervating the lateral rectus muscle (LR6). It is not the thinnest cranial nerve, as it contains more axons than the trochlear nerve.

 

Option D. X cranial nerve (Vagus nerve): The vagus nerve is a large, mixed nerve responsible for both sensory and motor functions in various body regions, making it much thicker compared to the trochlear nerve.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The fourth cranial nerve (trochlear nerve) is the thinnest cranial nerve due to its minimal number of axons, as it innervates only one muscle, the superior oblique muscle.

The central sulcus of Rolando is a prominent landmark on the lateral surface of the brain. It separates the frontal lobe from the parietal lobe and divides the precentral gyrus (motor cortex) from the postcentral gyrus (somatosensory cortex).

 

In the labeled image:

 

  • A is the pre-central sulcus, located anterior to the central sulcus.
  • B is the central sulcus of Rolando, correctly positioned between the precentral and postcentral gyri.
  • C is the post-central sulcus, located posterior to the central sulcus.
  • D represents the lateral sulcus (Sylvian fissure), a structure separating the frontal and temporal lobes.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The central sulcus of Rolando is the key landmark that separates the frontal lobe (motor cortex) from the parietal lobe (somatosensory cortex). It is labeled as B in this image.

questions.stem: Which nerve is most susceptible to get damage in head injury:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) VI cranial nerve

 

The sixth cranial nerve (abducens nerve) is the most susceptible to injury in cases of head trauma or raised intracranial tension (ICT). Several anatomical and functional factors make it vulnerable:

 

  1. Direct contact with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF): The sixth cranial nerve passes through the cisterna pontis, where it is in direct contact with CSF. Increased intracranial pressure can compress or displace the nerve, leading to damage.
  2. Multiple directional changes: The nerve changes direction multiple times along its course:
    • Exits from the pons, travels downward.
    • Moves anteriorly to pass through the cavernous sinus and then through the superior orbital fissure.
      These changes in direction create stress points, making it prone to injury during head trauma.
  3. Sharp edge of the petrous temporal bone: As the nerve travels along its course, it passes over the sharp edge of the petrous part of the temporal bone. Any trauma or sudden movement can cause compression or tearing at this site.
  4. Dorello’s canal: The nerve travels through Dorello's canal, a dural tunnel, before entering the cavernous sinus. The canal is a confined space, and any increase in pressure can compress the nerve.

 

Due to its long intracranial course and vulnerability at multiple anatomical points, the sixth cranial nerve is often injured in head trauma, raised ICT, or other conditions affecting the brain.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. I cranial nerve (Olfactory nerve): The olfactory nerve can be damaged in head injury, but it is less common compared to the sixth cranial nerve. Damage typically occurs due to fractures of the cribriform plate, leading to anosmia.

 

Option B. II cranial nerve (Optic nerve): The optic nerve is well-protected in its bony canal and is less likely to be injured compared to the abducens nerve unless there is severe trauma or direct orbital involvement.

 

Option D. X cranial nerve (Vagus nerve): The vagus nerve is located deeper and is relatively protected, making it less susceptible to direct injury from head trauma.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The sixth cranial nerve (abducens nerve) is the most commonly injured cranial nerve in head trauma, primarily due to:

 

  1. Its long intracranial course.
  2. Contact with CSF in the cisterna pontis.
  3. Vulnerability at the sharp edge of the petrous temporal bone.
  4. Passage through the confined Dorello’s canal.

 

Injury to this nerve typically results in lateral rectus palsy, causing horizontal diplopia.

questions.stemHtml: Which type of gland is depicted here?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Holocrine glands 

 

The image depicts a holocrine gland, which is a type of exocrine gland where the entire cell disintegrates to release its secretory product. These glands are primarily associated with sebaceous (oil) glands in the skin. The following features are characteristic of holocrine glands:

 

  1. Cell rupture: The cells accumulate their secretions and then undergo disintegration, releasing their contents.
  2. Sebaceous glands: These glands are typically located in the skin and associated with hair follicles, as seen in the image.
  3. Histological appearance: The image shows clusters of cells with clear vacuoles containing lipid material, characteristic of sebaceous glands.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Apocrine glands: These glands release their secretions by budding off the apical portion of the cell, commonly seen in specialized sweat glands. They are not shown in the image.

 

Option B. Merocrine glands: Merocrine glands (e.g., eccrine sweat glands) release their secretions via exocytosis without damaging the cell. The gland depicted does not have this appearance.

 

Option D. Endocrine glands: Endocrine glands release hormones directly into the bloodstream and lack ducts, unlike the gland shown in the image.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The gland shown in the image is a holocrine gland, specifically a sebaceous gland, characterized by the disintegration of cells to release oily secretions.

questions.stem: Your patient has lost the ability to discriminate between two points presented simultaneously to the skin. Your neurological evaluation is most likely to reveal a lesion in the
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Medial lemniscus

 

The medial lemniscus is part of the dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway, which is responsible for transmitting fine touch, proprioception, and two-point discrimination. This pathway begins with input from the fasciculus gracilis (lower limb). and fasciculus cuneatus (upper limb), which transmit sensory information to the medulla. From there, fibers decussate and ascend as the medial lemniscus to the thalamus and ultimately the sensory cortex.

 

A lesion in the medial lemniscus disrupts these sensory modalities, leading to deficits like the inability to perform two-point discrimination, a hallmark of dorsal column dysfunction.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Lateral lemniscus:The lateral lemniscus is part of the auditory pathway and plays no role in tactile sensation or two-point discrimination.

 

Option C. Spinal lemniscus: The spinal lemniscus transmits pain, temperature, and crude touch via the lateral and anterior spinothalamic tracts. It does not transmit fine touch or proprioception.

 

Option D. Trigeminal lemniscus: The trigeminal lemniscus is associated with sensory pathways for the face and is not responsible for two-point discrimination on the skin of the body.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The medial lemniscus is part of the dorsal column pathway, responsible for fine touch, proprioception, and two-point discrimination. Damage to this structure results in the loss of two-point discrimination ability.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman is being examined as a candidate for cosmetic breast surgery. The surgeon notes that both of her breasts sag considerably. Which structure has most likely become stretched to result in this condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Cooper’s ligaments

 

Cooper’s ligaments, also known as the suspensory ligaments of the breast, are connective tissue structures that support the breast and maintain its shape. They extend from the skin to the deep fascia overlying the pectoralis major muscle. When these ligaments become stretched or lose elasticity, the breasts may sag, a condition medically referred to as breast ptosis.

 

Stretching of Cooper's ligaments: With age, weight changes, or hormonal influences, these ligaments can stretch, leading to sagging of the breast tissue.

 

No involvement of muscles or fascia: Breast sagging is not related to the pectoralis major or minor muscles, nor to Scarpa’s fascia, as these structures do not provide direct structural support to the breast.

 

Clinical relevance in breast cancer:
 

Note: In breast cancer, fibrosis involving Cooper’s ligaments can result in skin dimpling, as the fibrosis pulls on these ligaments. This is different from sagging caused by simple ligament stretching.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Sagging of the breasts (breast ptosis) is primarily caused by the stretching of Cooper’s ligaments, which provide suspensory support to the breast tissue. These ligaments are crucial for maintaining the breast's shape and position.

Ans. D) Superior colliculus

 

The Nucleus of Edinger-Westphal is part of the oculomotor nerve (Cranial Nerve III) complex, located in the midbrain. It is responsible for parasympathetic innervation to the eye, controlling pupil constriction and lens accommodation.

 

The Edinger-Westphal nucleus is situated at the level of the superior colliculus in the midbrain. This colliculus is involved in visual reflexes and is a key anatomical landmark in transverse sections of the midbrain.

 

 

Other Options:

Option B. Fourth ventricle: The fourth ventricle is located in the pons and medulla oblongata, below the midbrain. It is not seen in sections at the level of the Edinger-Westphal nucleus.

 

Option C. Olive: The olive is part of the medulla oblongata and is associated with the inferior olivary nucleus. It is not present in the midbrain.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The Nucleus of Edinger-Westphal is located in the midbrain at the level of the superior colliculus, a structure associated with visual reflexes.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old female court stenographer is admitted to the orthopedic clinic with symptoms of carpal tunnel syndrome, with which she has suffered for almost a year. Which muscles most typically become weakened in this condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Thenar

 

Carpal tunnel syndrome involves compression of the median nerve as it passes through the carpal tunnel in the wrist. The median nerve innervates the thenar muscles, which are primarily responsible for thumb movements such as opposition, flexion, and abduction. These muscles are part of the thenar eminence, and their weakening is a hallmark of advanced carpal tunnel syndrome.

 

The thenar muscles supplied by the median nerve include:

 

  1. Abductor pollicis brevis
  2. Opponens pollicis
  3. Flexor pollicis brevis (superficial head)

 

Patients with long-standing carpal tunnel syndrome may exhibit weakness in these muscles, resulting in difficulty with thumb movements and, in severe cases, thenar muscle atrophy.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Dorsal interossei: These are innervated by the ulnar nerve and are responsible for finger abduction. They are unaffected in carpal tunnel syndrome.

 

Option B. Lumbricals III and IV: These are also innervated by the ulnar nerve. In carpal tunnel syndrome, only lumbricals I and II (innervated by the median nerve) may be affected.

 

Option D. Palmar interossei: Like the dorsal interossei, these are innervated by the ulnar nerve and contribute to finger adduction. They are not affected in carpal tunnel syndrome.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In carpal tunnel syndrome, compression of the median nerve typically weakens the thenar muscles, which control key thumb movements, such as opposition, flexion, and abduction.

questions.stem: Your patient has a stooped posture, shuffling gait, and a tremor in the fingers at rest. Which part of the brain will show neuronal degeneration?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Mesencephalon

 

The mesencephalon (midbrain) houses the substantia nigra, a critical structure involved in motor control. Degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra is the hallmark of Parkinson’s disease, which is characterized by symptoms such as a stooped posture, shuffling gait, bradykinesia, and resting tremor. The substantia nigra is part of the basal ganglia circuitry and plays a key role in regulating movement.

 

Other Options: 

 

Option A. Metencephalon: The metencephalon develops into the pons and cerebellum. While the cerebellum is involved in coordination, it is not directly implicated in Parkinson’s disease.

 

Option B. Diencephalon: The diencephalon gives rise to the thalamus and hypothalamus. While these structures are involved in sensory relay and autonomic functions, they are not the primary sites of degeneration in Parkinson’s disease.

 

Option D. Myelencephalon: The myelencephalon develops into the medulla oblongata, which is involved in autonomic functions like breathing and heart rate regulation. It is not associated with the symptoms or pathology of Parkinson’s disease.

 

Note:

 

 

Educational Objective:

 

Neuronal degeneration in Parkinson’s disease occurs in the substantia nigra, located in the mesencephalon (midbrain), which is responsible for producing dopamine crucial for motor control.

questions.stem: A patient has suffered a stroke caused by occlusion of the right anterior cerebral artery. This patient is most likely to present with

options.label: A
options.text: A loss of pain and temperature sensations in the left leg

options.label: C
options.text: Drooping of the corner of the mouth on the left

questions.answerText: A loss of pain and temperature sensations in the left leg
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) A loss of pain and temperature sensations in the left leg

 

The anterior cerebral artery (ACA). supplies the medial surface of the brain, including the areas of the primary motor and sensory cortices responsible for the lower limb. An occlusion of the right ACA affects the contralateral side (in this case, the left leg) due to the decussation of motor and sensory pathways.

 

  • The loss of pain and temperature sensations results from disruption of the sensory pathways supplying the contralateral lower limb.
  • Additionally, motor deficits such as weakness or paralysis of the contralateral lower limb can occur, but this is not the best fit based on the options provided.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Weakness of the right leg: This is incorrect because the right ACA supplies the medial surface of the right hemisphere, which corresponds to sensory and motor control of the left leg, not the right.

 

Option C. Drooping of the corner of the mouth on the left: Drooping of the corner of the mouth indicates a lower motor neuron lesion of the facial nerve or a lesion affecting the corticobulbar tracts. The ACA does not supply the areas responsible for facial movements; these are typically affected by middle cerebral artery (MCA) strokes.

 

Option D. A nonfluent aphasia: Nonfluent aphasia (Broca’s aphasia. occurs due to lesions in the left frontal lobe (Broca's area), which is supplied by the left MCA, not the ACA.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Occlusion of the anterior cerebral artery causes deficits in the contralateral lower limb due to its supply to the medial surface of the brain, which includes motor and sensory areas associated with the lower extremities. In this case, the loss of pain and temperature sensations in the left leg is the most likely clinical manifestation.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the papillae from the given histological section?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Circumvallate

 

The histological section shows features characteristic of circumvallate papillae. These are large, circular papillae that are surrounded by a trench. They are located at the back of the tongue and contain a significant number of taste buds. The circumvallate papillae are easily identified by their distinctive circular shape and the presence of a surrounding trench, which is a hallmark feature.

 

The image provided clearly shows this circular structure with trenches, confirming it as a circumvallate papilla.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Fungiform: Fungiform papillae are mushroom-shaped structures located on the dorsal surface of the tongue, mostly at the tip and sides. They are smaller than circumvallate papillae and lack the distinctive trench seen here.

 

Option C. Filiform: Filiform papillae are thin, elongated structures distributed across the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. These papillae do not contain taste buds, unlike the circumvallate papillae shown in the image.

 

Option D. Foliate: Foliate papillae are located on the lateral sides of the tongue and appear as folds. They are not circular or surrounded by trenches like circumvallate papillae.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Circumvallate papillae are large, circular structures surrounded by trenches and contain numerous taste buds. Filiform papillae are the only papillae that lack taste buds.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the cell marked in the histological image of the cerebellum shown below:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Purkinje cells

 

The marked cell in the histological image is a Purkinje cell, which is a distinct feature of the cerebellum. These cells are characterized by their large size and prominent location at the interface between the molecular layer and the granular layer of the cerebellar cortex. Purkinje cells have a highly branched dendritic tree extending into the molecular layer, and they are inhibitory in function, sending GABAergic signals to the deep cerebellar nuclei.

 

The cerebellum is organized into three layers:

 

  1. Molecular layer: Contains dendritic trees of Purkinje cells and axons of granule cells.
  2. Purkinje cell layer: Consists of the large Purkinje cell bodies, which are clearly visible in the image.
  3. Granular layer: Contains densely packed small granule cells.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Basket cells: These are interneurons found in the molecular layer of the cerebellum. They are much smaller and form synaptic connections with Purkinje cells, but they do not resemble the marked large cell in the image.

 

Option C. Golgi cells: These interneurons are located in the granular layer and are involved in modulating signals from granule cells. They are smaller and do not have the prominent, large cell body seen in Purkinje cells.

 

Option D. Granule cells: These are small and densely packed cells located in the granular layer. They do not have the size or morphology of the marked cell.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Purkinje cells are large, inhibitory neurons located in the cerebellar cortex, forming a distinct layer between the molecular and granular layers.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the type of cartilage shown in the image below:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Elastic cartilage

 

The image shows a type of cartilage with densely packed chondrocytes in lacunae and a matrix that is rich in elastic fibers. These elastic fibers appear as thin, dark, and wavy structures in the extracellular matrix, which is the defining feature of elastic cartilage. Elastic cartilage provides flexible support and is commonly found in structures such as the external ear, epiglottis, and Eustachian tube.

 

Key distinguishing features:

 

  • Presence of elastic fibers: Seen as dark-staining fibers in the matrix.
  • Chondrocytes in lacunae: Grouped together in nests, indicating cartilage.
  • Non-homogenous matrix: Unlike hyaline cartilage, which has a smooth, glassy matrix, elastic cartilage has a fibrous appearance.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Hyaline cartilage: Hyaline cartilage has a homogenous, glassy matrix without visible fibers. It is found in areas like the nose, trachea, and ends of long bones. The fibrous appearance in the image excludes this option.

 

 

Option C. Articular cartilage: A subtype of hyaline cartilage, articular cartilage covers joint surfaces. It lacks visible elastic fibers, making it distinct from elastic cartilage.

 

Option D. Fibrocartilage: Fibrocartilage is characterized by thick bundles of collagen fibers, which appear as dense, wavy, red-staining fibers under the microscope. This feature is not seen in the given image.

 

 

Educational Objective:

 

Elastic cartilage contains elastic fibers in its matrix, providing flexibility and resilience, and is found in structures like the external ear and epiglottis.

questions.stemHtml: All of the following are Not true about Given Histology ?

options.label: A
options.text: The cortical portion is mainly composed of lymphocytes

options.label: C
options.text: It is derived from the fourth Pharyngeal pouch

questions.answerText: It is derived from the fourth Pharyngeal pouch
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) It is derived from the fourth Pharyngeal pouch

 

The histological image shows the thymus, a lymphoid organ characterized by its lobular architecture. The lobules are separated by connective tissue septa. The cortex is densely packed with lymphocytes, and the medulla contains eosinophilic structures known as Hassall's corpuscles, which are unique to the thymus. These features confirm the organ as the thymus.

 

Key facts:

 

  1. The cortex of the thymus contains numerous lymphocytes, giving it a dark-staining appearance.
  2. The medulla contains Hassall's corpuscles, which are composed of epithelial cells and are a hallmark feature of the thymus.
  3. The thymus is derived from the third pharyngeal pouch during embryogenesis.
  4. The thymus undergoes atrophy after puberty, with much of the tissue being replaced by fat.

 

It is derived from the fourth Pharyngeal pouch: This is incorrect. The thymus is derived from the third pharyngeal pouch, not the fourth. This makes it the correct answer to the "not true" question.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. The cortical portion is mainly composed of lymphocytes: This is correct. The cortex is densely populated with lymphocytes, which gives it a basophilic (blue) appearance under the microscope.

 

Option B. The medulla contains Hassall's corpuscles: This is correct. Hassall's corpuscles are present in the medulla and are unique to the thymus.

 

Option D. It undergoes atrophy puberty onwards: This is correct. The thymus degenerates after puberty, and much of its functional tissue is replaced by adipose tissue.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The thymus is derived from the third pharyngeal pouch, contains Hassall's corpuscles in the medulla, and undergoes atrophy after puberty.

 

Note:

questions.stemHtml: Shown epithelium is found in ?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Urinary bladder

 

The image shows transitional epithelium (also called urothelium), which is a specialized epithelium found in the urinary system. This epithelium is characterized by:

 

  • Stratification: Multiple layers of cells.
  • Surface cells with dome-shaped appearance: The superficial cells (umbrella cells) appear dome-shaped in a relaxed state and can flatten when the bladder is distended.
  • Binucleated cells: Often, the cells in the uppermost layer (umbrella cells) have two nuclei, a feature seen here.
  • Function: Urothelium provides a protective barrier and accommodates stretching and distension of the urinary tract.

 

This type of epithelium lines the urinary bladder, ureters, and the upper urethra, making it unique to the urinary system.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Stomach: The stomach is lined with simple columnar epithelium, which does not show the stratified or dome-shaped appearance seen here.

 

 

Option B. Lungs: The respiratory tract contains pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells, which is distinct from the transitional epithelium.

 

 

Option C. Liver: The liver does not have epithelial linings like the one shown in the image. Instead, it is composed of hepatocytes arranged in plates.

 

 

Educational Objective:

 

Transitional epithelium (urothelium) is a stratified epithelium with dome-shaped, sometimes binucleated cells, found in the urinary bladder and other parts of the urinary tract.

questions.stem: The movements at the _________________ joint permit a person to look
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Atlanto-axial

 

The atlanto-axial joint is a synovial joint located between the first cervical vertebra (C1 or atlas) and the second cervical vertebra (C2 or axis). This joint is responsible for the "no" movement of the head, allowing rotation of the head from side to side. This rotation occurs because of the articulation between the odontoid process (dens) of C2 and the anterior arch of C1.

 

 

In contrast, the atlanto-occipital joint allows for the "yes" movement of the head (flexion and extension) and does not contribute to lateral or rotational movements.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Atlanto-occipital: This joint allows for flexion and extension movements of the head (nodding "yes") but does not permit rotation.

 

Option C. C2-C3: This joint is a typical intervertebral joint that allows minimal movement and contributes to stability rather than significant rotation.

 

Option D. C3-C4: Similar to C2-C3, this is another typical intervertebral joint with limited movement, primarily flexion and extension.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The atlanto-axial joint allows rotational movement of the head (the "no" motion), enabling a person to look to the right and left.

questions.stemHtml: A 40-year-old male patient presents with a swelling that has been slowly growing in the past 2 years. On examination, it was variable in consistency and fully mobile. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Parotid tumor

 

The swelling in this case is located just below the ear and is described as slowly growing, variable in consistency, and fully mobile. These are classic features of a parotid tumor, which is the most likely diagnosis in this scenario. Parotid tumors are commonly benign (e.g., pleomorphic adenoma. but can occasionally be malignant. They usually present as a painless, slow-growing mass in the region of the parotid gland.

 

Key characteristics:

 

  • Location: Near the angle of the jaw, below the ear, consistent with the anatomical location of the parotid gland.
  • Variable consistency: Suggests a tumor rather than a cyst or lymph node.
  • Mobility: Parotid tumors are often mobile unless they invade surrounding structures.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Dermoid cyst: Dermoid cysts are usually found in midline locations (e.g., periorbital region) and are not commonly seen in the parotid region. They are also more common in younger individuals.

 

 

Option C. Sebaceous cyst: While sebaceous cysts can occur in the region of the parotid gland, they are usually smaller, superficial, and have a more characteristic fluctuant consistency. They often involve a central punctum, which is not described here.

 

 

Option D. Cervical lymph node: Lymph node enlargement due to infection or malignancy typically presents with a firm, fixed consistency. The location and mobile nature of the swelling make this less likely.

 

 

Educational Objective:

 

A slowly growing, mobile swelling near the parotid gland in an adult is most likely a parotid tumor. Proper evaluation, including imaging and possible biopsy, is necessary to confirm the diagnosis.

questions.stem: A patient presents with sudden onset of chest pain shooting to the neck and interscapular region. X-ray shows widened mediastinum. BP is 110/90 mmHg in the right upper limb and 160/100 mmHg in the left upper limb. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Acute aortic dissection

 

The clinical presentation of sudden onset chest pain radiating to the neck and interscapular region, along with a widened mediastinum on X-ray and significant blood pressure discrepancy between the limbs, strongly suggests an acute aortic dissection.

 

 

Key points:

 

  • Chest pain pattern: Acute aortic dissection typically causes severe, tearing or ripping chest pain that radiates to the neck, back, or interscapular region due to the pathway of the aorta.
  • Widened mediastinum: A classic radiologic finding associated with aortic dissection.
  • Blood pressure difference: This occurs due to involvement of the aortic branches, causing obstruction or malperfusion in one of the arteries (e.g., subclavian artery), leading to differential blood pressure readings.

 

Aortic dissection is a medical emergency requiring immediate diagnosis and intervention to prevent complications such as rupture or end-organ ischemia.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Acute coronary syndrome: While acute coronary syndrome (e.g., myocardial infarction) can present with sudden chest pain, it typically refers pain to the front of the chest, arm, or jaw. It does not cause back or interscapular pain, nor is it associated with a widened mediastinum or blood pressure discrepancies.

 

Option B. Acute pulmonary embolism: Pulmonary embolism can cause sudden chest pain, but the pain is usually pleuritic in nature and often associated with shortness of breath, hypoxia, and tachycardia. It does not explain the widened mediastinum or blood pressure differences.

 

Option D. Esophageal rupture: Also known as Boerhaave syndrome, this condition can present with severe chest pain and a widened mediastinum due to air or fluid leakage. However, it typically follows vomiting or esophageal injury and does not cause blood pressure discrepancies or radiation of pain to the interscapular region.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Acute aortic dissection presents with sudden, tearing chest pain radiating to the neck and back, widened mediastinum on imaging, and blood pressure discrepancies between limbs. Immediate diagnosis and intervention are critical.

questions.stemHtml: A 50-year-old patient with a history of trauma one week back presents with confusion and ataxia. He is on treatment for alcohol dependence and his last intake was 2 weeks back. CT scan reveals the following finding. What is the diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Subdural hemorrhage

 

The CT scan reveals a crescent-shaped (banana-shapeD. hyperdense collection on one side of the brain, which is a classic appearance of a subdural hemorrhage (SDH). Subdural hemorrhage occurs due to the tearing of bridging veins, often following trauma.

 

Key clinical features:

 

  1. Delayed presentation: SDH may present days to weeks after trauma, as in this case where the patient presents one week later with confusion and ataxia.
  2. Risk factors: Alcohol dependence is a common risk factor due to associated brain atrophy, which stretches the veins, making them more prone to injury.
  3. CT imaging: Crescent-shaped hemorrhage conforming to the brain surface is typical of SDH, unlike extradural hemorrhage (EDH), which has a biconvex (lens-shapeD. appearance.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Extradural hemorrhage: EDH is typically associated with a lens-shaped collection on CT. It often results from middle meningeal artery rupture and presents with a lucid interval followed by rapid deterioration, unlike the delayed presentation of SDH.

 

 

Option C. Intra-parenchymal hemorrhage: This appears as a focal hyperdensity within the brain parenchyma, usually from hypertension, trauma, or hemorrhagic stroke. The crescent shape on the CT excludes this diagnosis.

 

Option D. Subarachnoid hemorrhage: SAH presents with hyperdensity in the basal cisterns or sulci, and it is commonly associated with a "thunderclap headache." The CT findings in this case are inconsistent with SAH.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Subdural hemorrhage appears as a crescent-shaped collection on CT, often occurring after trauma due to the tearing of bridging veins. It may present with delayed symptoms, particularly in high-risk individuals like those with alcohol dependence or brain atrophy.

questions.stemHtml: A 23-year-old male patient presents with midline swelling in the neck. The swelling moves with deglutition and protrusion of the tongue. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Thyroglossal cyst

 

A thyroglossal cyst is the most likely diagnosis in a patient presenting with a midline neck swelling that moves with both deglutition (swallowing) and protrusion of the tongue. This cyst results from the persistence of the thyroglossal duct, which is an embryological remnant of the thyroid gland's descent from the foramen cecum at the base of the tongue to its final position in the neck.

 

Key clinical features:

 

  1. Location: Thyroglossal cysts are midline structures, often near the hyoid bone.
  2. Movement with swallowing and tongue protrusion: Due to its attachment to the thyroglossal tract.
  3. Presentation: Typically presents in young individuals as a painless, cystic swelling.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Brachial cyst: These are lateral neck swellings found anterior to the sternocleidomastoid muscle. They do not move with swallowing or tongue protrusion, making this diagnosis unlikely.

 

 

Option C. Plunging ranula: A ranula is a salivary cyst that arises from the sublingual gland. It presents as a swelling in the floor of the mouth, not in the midline of the neck.

 

 

Option D. Dermoid cyst: While dermoid cysts can occur in the midline, they do not move with deglutition or tongue protrusion and are not associated with the thyroglossal duct.

 

 

Educational Objective:

 

A thyroglossal cyst is a midline neck swelling that moves with swallowing and tongue protrusion due to its attachment to the thyroglossal duct, a remnant of thyroid gland embryogenesis.

questions.stem: Cardiac dominance is decided by:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Posterior interventricular artery 

 

Cardiac dominance is determined by the artery that gives rise to the posterior interventricular artery (PIVA), which supplies the posterior part of the interventricular septum.

 

  1. Right cardiac dominance (90% of the population): The posterior interventricular artery originates from the right coronary artery.
  2. Left cardiac dominance (10% of the population): The posterior interventricular artery originates from the left coronary artery.
  3. Co-dominance: In a small percentage of people, the posterior interventricular artery receives blood supply from both the right and left coronary arteries.

 

Thus, the posterior interventricular artery is the key structure used to define cardiac dominance.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Anterior interventricular artery: This artery (also known as the left anterior descending artery) arises from the left coronary artery and supplies the anterior part of the interventricular septum. It does not determine cardiac dominance.

 

Option C. Right coronary artery: While right dominance is common, dominance itself is not determined by the artery but by the origin of the posterior interventricular artery.

 

Option D. Left coronary artery: Similar to the right coronary artery, dominance is determined by whether the posterior interventricular artery arises from the left coronary artery.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Cardiac dominance is decided by the artery that gives rise to the posterior interventricular artery. Right coronary dominance is most common, occurring in 90% of individuals.

questions.stem: A tumor of the uncinate process of the pancreas affects which of the following vessels?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Superior mesenteric artery

 

The uncinate process of the pancreas is the portion of the pancreas that projects posteriorly and lies behind the superior mesenteric vessels. A tumor in this region is likely to compress or involve the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) and its accompanying vein because these structures are closely related anatomically.

 

 

  • The superior mesenteric artery and vein pass anterior to the uncinate process of the pancreas.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Portal vein: The portal vein forms posterior to the neck of the pancreas, not at the uncinate process. Hence, it is not the vessel primarily affected.

 

Option C. Common hepatic artery: This artery is a branch of the celiac trunk and is not closely related to the uncinate process of the pancreas.

 

Option D. Inferior mesenteric artery: This artery arises from the abdominal aorta below the superior mesenteric artery and is unrelated to the pancreas or its uncinate process.

 

Educational Objective:

 

A tumor in the uncinate process of the pancreas primarily affects the superior mesenteric artery and vein due to their close anatomical relationship.

questions.stem: A patient presented with clinical features of ataxia and incoordination. This is due to thrombosis of which artery?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Superior cerebellar

 

Ataxia and incoordination are clinical features indicative of cerebellar dysfunction, as the cerebellum is responsible for coordinating balance, posture, and motor activity. Thrombosis or occlusion of the superior cerebellar artery (SCA), which supplies the superior portion of the cerebellum, leads to these symptoms.

 

Key points:

 

  • The superior cerebellar artery arises from the basilar artery and supplies the upper part of the cerebellum, as well as parts of the midbrain.
  • Cerebellar artery occlusion can cause ataxia, dysmetria, and difficulty coordinating movements.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Posterior cerebral: Supplies the occipital lobe and parts of the temporal lobe, primarily causing visual deficits if occluded.

 

Option B. Middle cerebral: Supplies the lateral cerebral cortex and deep structures such as the basal ganglia. Its occlusion typically results in contralateral motor and sensory deficits, not ataxia.

 

Option C. Internal carotid: Supplies the anterior and middle cerebral arteries, and thrombosis here would cause widespread cerebral ischemia but not isolated cerebellar symptoms.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Thrombosis of the superior cerebellar artery leads to ataxia and incoordination due to ischemia of the cerebellum, which is responsible for balance and motor coordination.
questions.stemHtml: A patient presented with clinical features of ataxia and incoordination. This is due to thrombosis of which artery?

questions.stem: Nerve of anterior compartment of thigh is.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Femoral nerve

 

The femoral nerve is the primary nerve supplying the anterior compartment of the thigh. This nerve arises from the lumbar plexus (L2-L4) and innervates muscles in the anterior compartment, which are responsible for knee extension and hip flexion. The main muscles in this compartment include the quadriceps femoris, sartorius, and iliopsoas.

 

Key points:

 

  • Motor function: Supplies muscles involved in extending the knee (quadriceps femoris) and flexing the hip.
  • Sensory function: Provides sensation to the anterior thigh and medial leg via the saphenous nerve.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Obturator nerve: This nerve supplies the medial compartment of the thigh, which is responsible for thigh adduction.

 

Option C. Sciatic nerve: This nerve supplies the posterior compartment of the thigh and is involved in knee flexion and hip extension.

 

Option D. Tibial nerve: This nerve innervates the posterior compartment of the leg and foot, playing a role in plantarflexion.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The femoral nerve is the key nerve of the anterior compartment of the thigh, responsible for knee extension and hip flexion.

questions.stem: A patient presented with the extension of MCP joint and flexion of IP joints. Which muscle is affected?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Interossei and lumbricals

 

The interossei and lumbricals are responsible for fine motor movements of the fingers, particularly the coordination of flexion at the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints and extension at the interphalangeal (IP) joints. Damage or dysfunction of these muscles leads to the "claw hand" deformity, characterized by the extension of the MCP joints and flexion of the IP joints due to the unopposed action of the extrinsic muscles (flexor digitorum profundus and extensor digitorum).

 

Key points:

 

  • Normal function: The lumbricals and interossei flex the MCP joints and extend the IP joints, maintaining the delicate "pen-holding" or "writing" position of the fingers.
  • Claw hand: When these muscles are damaged (e.g., due to ulnar or median nerve injury), the opposite occurs: extension of MCP joints and flexion of IP joints.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Extensor digitorum: This muscle extends the MCP and IP joints but is not responsible for the specific deformity described.

 

Option C. Abductor pollicis: This muscle is involved in thumb abduction and does not affect the MCP or IP joints of the fingers.

 

Option D. Abductor pollicis brevis: This muscle is also specific to thumb abduction and unrelated to the deformity described.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The interossei and lumbricals are crucial for coordinated flexion at MCP joints and extension at IP joints. Their dysfunction results in claw hand deformity, with extension at MCP joints and flexion at IP joints.

questions.stem: The long left recurrent laryngeal nerve is due to the persistence of which arch artery?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) 6th arch

 

The long left recurrent laryngeal nerve is due to the persistence of the 6th pharyngeal arch artery. During embryological development:

 

  • On the right side, the 6th arch artery disappears, allowing the right recurrent laryngeal nerve to loop around the right subclavian artery.
  • On the left side, the 6th arch artery persists as the ductus arteriosus (which later becomes the ligamentum arteriosum). This causes the left recurrent laryngeal nerve to loop around the arch of the aorta and remain longer than its counterpart on the right side.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. 3rd arch: This arch gives rise to parts of the common carotid artery and the internal carotid artery, not related to the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

 

Option B. 4th arch: The 4th arch contributes to the arch of the aorta on the left side and the right subclavian artery on the right side but does not directly influence the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

 

Option C. 5th arch: This arch is either rudimentary or does not develop in humans, so it has no role in the development of the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The long left recurrent laryngeal nerve is due to the persistence of the 6th pharyngeal arch artery, which forms the ductus arteriosus (later ligamentum arteriosum).
