questions.stem: SSA fibres are present in which of the following cranial nerves?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) I, II, VIII 

 

Special Somatic Afferent (SSA. fibers are sensory fibers that carry information related to vision, hearing, and balance. They are specific to cranial nerves associated with the special senses. These fibers are present in the following cranial nerves:

 

  1. Cranial Nerve I (Olfactory nerve): Responsible for the sense of smell.
  2. Cranial Nerve II (Optic nerve): Responsible for vision.
  3. Cranial Nerve VIII (Vestibulocochlear nerve): Responsible for hearing (cochlear component) and balance (vestibular component).

 

These are the only cranial nerves containing SSA fibers, as they are involved in specialized sensory functions.

 

Educational Objective:

 

SSA fibers are found in cranial nerves I (Olfactory), II (Optic), and VIII (Vestibulocochlear), as they are responsible for the special senses of smell, vision, hearing, and balance.

questions.stem: Which of the following cranial nerves nuclei shows SSA features
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) VIII 

 

The Special Somatic Afferent (SSA. features are associated with sensory functions for vision, hearing, and balance. Among the cranial nerves, Cranial Nerve VIII (Vestibulocochlear nerve) contains nuclei that are classified as SSA because they are involved in the special senses of hearing (cochlear nucleus) and balance (vestibular nucleus).

 

Key details:

 

  • Cranial Nerve VIII (Vestibulocochlear):
    • Nuclei: Cochlear nucleus (for hearing) and vestibular nucleus (for balance).
    • These nuclei process sensory information received through SSA fibers.
  • Cranial Nerves I and II (Olfactory and Optic): These cranial nerves carry SSA fibers but do not have nuclei, as their sensory information is processed directly by the olfactory bulb (I) and retina (II), which are part of the central nervous system.
  • Cranial Nerve VII (Facial nerve): The facial nerve does not contain SSA features; it primarily has motor, parasympathetic, and general sensory components.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Among cranial nerves, only Cranial Nerve VIII (Vestibulocochlear nerve) has nuclei (cochlear and vestibular) that exhibit SSA features for hearing and balance.

questions.stem: GSE fibres are present in cranial nerves:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) III, IV, VI, XII

 

General Somatic Efferent (GSE) fibers are motor fibers that supply the skeletal muscles derived from somites. These fibers are involved in voluntary motor control. The cranial nerves that contain GSE fibers and their respective muscles include:

 

  • Cranial Nerve III (Oculomotor nerve): Innervates most of the extraocular muscles, including the superior rectus, inferior rectus, medial rectus, and inferior oblique, as well as the levator palpebrae superioris.
  • Cranial Nerve IV (Trochlear nerve): Supplies the superior oblique muscle of the eye.
  • Cranial Nerve VI (Abducens nerve): Innervates the lateral rectus muscle of the eye.
  • Cranial Nerve XII (Hypoglossal nerve): Supplies the intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the tongue.

 

These cranial nerves have motor nuclei that are classified as GSE.

 

Educational Objective:

 

GSE fibers are found in cranial nerves III (Oculomotor), IV (Trochlear), VI (Abducens), and XII (Hypoglossal), as they control skeletal muscles derived from somites.

questions.stem: Which of the following are branches of the anterior division of the internal iliac artery? Superior gluteal arteryInferior gluteal arterySuperior vesical arteryMiddle rectal arteryInferior vesical arteryVaginal artery
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) 2, 3, 4, 5, 6

 

The internal iliac artery is divided into anterior and posterior divisions. The anterior division primarily supplies the pelvic organs, perineum, and parts of the lower limb, while the posterior division supplies the gluteal and spinal regions.

 

Branches of the Anterior Division of the Internal Iliac Artery:

 

  1. Inferior gluteal artery (2): Supplies the gluteal region, exiting the pelvis below the piriformis.
  2. Superior vesical artery (3): Supplies the bladder.
  3. Middle rectal artery (4): Supplies the rectum.
  4. Inferior vesical artery (5) (in males) or vaginal artery (6) (in females): Supplies the bladder and nearby structures (e.g., prostate in males or vagina in females).

 

Note: 

 

Branches of the Posterior Division:

 

Mnemonic: I Love Sunny

 

  1. I: Iliolumbar artery
  2. L: Lateral sacral artery
  3. S: Superior gluteal artery

 

The superior gluteal artery (1) is the largest branch of the posterior division and exits the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen above the piriformis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The anterior division of the internal iliac artery supplies the pelvic cavity (bladder, rectum, vagina, prostate) and includes branches such as the inferior gluteal, superior vesical, middle rectal, inferior vesical, and vaginal arteries.

questions.stemHtml: Fibers from the marked structure end in which of the following areas of the thalamus?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Anterior nucleus

 

The structure marked in the image is the mammillary body, a part of the hypothalamus. It plays a key role in the Papez circuit, which is associated with memory and emotional processing. The Papez circuit involves several brain structures:

 

  1. Hippocampus: Sends fibers via the fornix.
  2. Fornix: Transmits signals to the mammillary body.
  3. Mammillary body: Sends impulses to the anterior nucleus of the thalamus through the mammillothalamic tract.
  4. Anterior nucleus of the thalamus: Relays these signals to the cingulate gyrus for further processing.

 

In this circuit, the mammillary body acts as a relay station, and the fibers from the mammillary body terminate in the anterior nucleus of the thalamus. This connection is crucial for the limbic system, which regulates emotional states and memory consolidation.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Posterior nucleus: The posterior nucleus of the thalamus is not directly involved in the Papez circuit. It plays a role in sensory processing, including nociception (pain perception).

 

Option B. Reticular nucleus: The reticular nucleus modulates thalamic activity but does not serve as a termination point for fibers from the mammillary body. Its primary role is in attention and sensory filtering.

 

Option D. Ventral lateral nucleus: The ventral lateral nucleus of the thalamus is associated with motor control, receiving input from the cerebellum and basal ganglia. It is unrelated to the limbic structures or the Papez circuit.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The Papez circuit connects the mammillary body to the anterior nucleus of the thalamus, which is involved in memory and emotional processing.

questions.stemHtml: A 48-year-old female patient presented with recurrent episodes of severe abdominal pain, which is often accompanied by nausea and vomiting. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy reveals multiple peptic ulcers in the duodenal bulb. Laboratory tests show elevated gastrin levels. She was given Prilosec for a long time. She was also consuming a vegetarian diet and now presented with tiredness & palpitations since a month. She complained of progressive sensory loss in her lower extremities. Neurological examination reveals impaired vibratory sensation in both legs. An MRI of the spinal cord shows no structural abnormalities. On blood examination she had following haematological slide was found. All of the following statements are correct in this case except:

options.label: A
options.text: This is a case of gastrinoma with high gastrin secretion resulting in hypersecretion of hydrochloric acid.

options.label: B
options.text: Prilosec is an example of a proton pump inhibitor which may cause decrease Vit B12 absorption.

options.label: C
options.text: In this patient due to Vitamin B 12 deficiency myelination of anterior spinothalamic tract has been affected.

options.label: D
options.text: On haematological examination Increased mean corpuscular volume (MCV, >100 fL) and mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH) and polymorphonuclear cells with multiple lobes are found.

questions.answerText: In this patient due to Vitamin B 12 deficiency myelination of anterior spinothalamic tract has been affected.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) In this patient due to Vitamin B 12 deficiency myelination of anterior spinothalamic tract has been affected. 

 

Vitamin B12 deficiency commonly causes subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord, which primarily affects the dorsal column pathways (fasciculus gracilis and fasciculus cuneatus) responsible for proprioception and vibratory sensation. The anterior spinothalamic tract, which carries crude touch and pressure, is typically not affected in Vitamin B12 deficiency.

 

This patient presents with a gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome) and associated Vitamin B12 deficiency. 

 

Proton pump inhibitors (like PriloseC. used to manage hypersecretion of gastric acid in Zollinger-Ellison syndrome can impair Vitamin B12 absorption over time.

 

This occurs because intrinsic factor, necessary for B12 absorption, relies on an acidic gastric environment.

 

The patient's hematological findings, including macrocytic anemia (MCV >100 fL) and hypersegmented neutrophils, are characteristic of megaloblastic anemia, often caused by Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Vitamin B12 deficiency commonly causes subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord, primarily affecting the dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis and fasciculus cuneatus) and not the anterior spinothalamic tract. Hematological findings often include macrocytic anemia and hypersegmented neutrophils.

questions.stemHtml: A 21-year-old null gravida caucasian patient presented with a 15-month history of amenorrhea, bifrontal headache, and photophobia. Examination revealed general physical, neurologic, and ophthalmoscopic findings with normal visual fields. A pelvic examination revealed normal external genitalia, nulliparous cervix and uterus, and bilateral cystic ovarian masses measuring 8 cm in diameter on the right and 4 cm on the left. Endocrine evaluation revealed an elevated serum prolactin in the range of 48 to 50 ng/ml. This situation was related with mass in the following area of the below image
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) B

 

The clinical presentation of this patient, including amenorrhea, galactorrhea, elevated serum prolactin levels, and headache, points to a diagnosis of prolactinoma, the most common type of pituitary adenoma. The mass is located in the pituitary gland, which is housed within the sella turcica, a saddle-shaped depression in the sphenoid bone (labeled as B in the image).

 

  • Prolactinomas are pituitary tumors that secrete prolactin, leading to hyperprolactinemia. Elevated prolactin levels suppress gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), resulting in hypogonadism, amenorrhea, and infertility in women.
  • The bifrontal headache and photophobia are likely due to the mass effect of the tumor. Larger adenomas can compress the optic chiasm, causing bitemporal hemianopia, although visual fields were reported as normal in this case.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. A: Incorrect. This region corresponds to the cribriform plate and is not involved in pituitary tumors or related endocrinological syndromes.

 

Option C. C: Incorrect. This area represents the foramen magnum. Tumors in this region would involve the brainstem or spinal cord, leading to entirely different symptoms, such as cranial nerve deficits or motor dysfunction.

 

Option D. D: Incorrect. This represents the clivus. Lesions in the clival region typically include chordomas or other bony tumors, not pituitary adenomas.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The pituitary gland, located in the sella turcica (B), is the site of prolactinomas, which are the most common cause of hyperprolactinemia, leading to galactorrhea, amenorrhea, and infertility. This region can be surgically accessed via a transnasal transsphenoidal approach for treatment when needed.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the marked structure:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Accessory nerve

 

The marked structure is the accessory nerve (cranial nerve XI). It emerges from the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid (SCM) muscle and runs obliquely across the posterior triangle of the neck, toward the trapezius muscle. The accessory nerve has both cranial and spinal roots, with the spinal root innervating the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles.

 

  • The accessory nerve is easily identified in the posterior triangle because of its oblique course and its importance in motor innervation. Damage to this nerve can lead to weakness of the trapezius, causing drooping of the shoulder and difficulty raising the arm above the horizontal plane.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Transverse cervical nerve: Incorrect. The transverse cervical nerve is a sensory nerve that runs horizontally across the neck and supplies the skin over the anterior cervical triangle. It does not innervate muscles and has a different trajectory.

 

Option B. Lesser occipital nerve: Incorrect. The lesser occipital nerve is a sensory nerve that ascends along the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid, supplying the skin of the scalp in the occipital region. It does not run obliquely through the posterior triangle.

 

Option C. Great auricular nerve: Incorrect. The great auricular nerve runs vertically across the sternocleidomastoid toward the angle of the mandible and the external ear, providing sensory innervation. It does not have the same oblique trajectory toward the trapezius.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The accessory nerve (cranial nerve XI) runs obliquely in the posterior triangle of the neck, providing motor innervation to the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles. Damage to this nerve can impair shoulder elevation and neck movements.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the marked structure?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Ostium of left coronary artery

 

The image shows a superior view of the heart, with the aorta and pulmonary trunk sectioned to expose the internal structures. The marked structure corresponds to the ostium (opening) of the left coronary artery, which is located within the left coronary sinus of the aorta, just above the left cusp of the aortic valve.

 

  • The aortic valve has three cusps: left coronary cusp, right coronary cusp, and non-coronary cusp. The ostium of the left coronary artery lies in the left coronary cusp, allowing blood to flow into the left coronary artery during diastole when the valve is closed.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Auricle of right atrium: Incorrect. The auricle of the right atrium is an external structure and is not visible in this superior cross-sectional view of the heart.

 

Option C. Posterior cusp of aortic valve: Incorrect. The posterior cusp of the aortic valve is also referred to as the non-coronary cusp. While visible in this view, the marked structure does not correspond to this cusp.

 

Option D. Pulmonary trunk: Incorrect. The pulmonary trunk is visible in the superior view of the heart, but the marked structure is within the aorta and does not correspond to the pulmonary trunk.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The ostium of the left coronary artery is located within the left coronary sinus of the aortic valve and plays a critical role in supplying oxygenated blood to the heart via the left coronary artery.
